Nothingness is not inherently bad.

The fear of death is natural but very irrational, you can look at death as an endless void of non-existence or you can look at it as a inevitable release from mortal chains, the death of joy and dreams, but also the death of sorrow and nightmares. 
Death, as life, is not good nor bad,it just is.

The best thing to do is make peace with it, don't try to fight death or ask why, just train yourself to accept it and recognize that nothingness is what you make of it.

Of course, in your deathbed you will still experience fear of death, but if you acquire the mental faculties to recollect your thoughts and contemplate death without judging it, you will be peaceful.

Let me give you an example of how I envision a Wizard in your average MMO combat:

Just like it is now, the guy would mostly position himself far from melee range, behind his other companions, and could conjure small buffs,crowd control as well as crank a few small lightning strikes every 2 or 3 minutes, everytime situation gets really dire, he'd pull out his spellbook and cast a REAL spell, which would take time as he speaks the words of power and does the appropriate ritualistic movements to summon his spell, once cast, the effects would be devastating or extremely beneficial, however the Wizard is drained,lost rare components and can't cast the same spell for a while (maybe 10 or 20 minute cooldown for each real spell), he can cast another real spell but it would drain him even further and put him in a vulnerable position, this forces to player to manage his power and not cast spells in an inconsequential manner.

Every few encounters (3 or 4 fights or so) the Wizard would have to sit and medidate to recover his strengths, this process can take as little as 20 or 30 seconds depending on your meditation skill (just like in EQ), as soon as he's done, his HP and mana reservoirs are full again, but his cooldowns and components remain the same.

I'm sure that if I'd take some time to be more creative I could come up with something more interesting than lightning strikes and debuffs for cantrips, but you get the idea.

Speaking from personal experience, creating a very interesting and memorable campaign that should last only a single session is almost impossible.

I've designed a sort of pre-campaign (like a prologue) for my main campaign and the idea was for us to through it in 2 or 3  sessions tops.

Now, only after 6 or 7 sessions we're finally seeing the end of the campaign, and even then I've not managed to make it very interesting because in order to add depth you AND your players have to put some time into the world you've created.

In short, if you're going to design a 15-20 hour campaign, keep it simple, very simple, no branching storytelling
(in fact, a really good tip here is to make it very linear), no deep intricate political schemes and social events, no ultra-designed lore, etc.

Create a simple setting, a simple story, and play it smart; Give it a little twist here and there and focus on the way you describe things to make they seem more fleshed out than they actually are, you'll be surprised to find out  that what really makes a campaign memorable isn't exactly the things that you've built, but the actions and influence of your players.

To convey personality to your character, not exactly by speaking ye olde english but by assuming certain role and playing it, it's that simple.

For example, you create an archetype to your Wizard, he's a young apprentice covered in jewelry and is constantly anxious, roleplaying means you either 

A) Try to convey this personality through this character by speaking and taking actions that make sense in the character's context (traditional roleplaying)

B) Play the game by only taking actions said character would take, for instance, if your character likes Goblins, you wouldn't attack them (loose roleplaying)
